abstract:
Chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.) is the second most widely grown legume crop after soybean. Here,
we measured the macronutrients and performed proteome profiling of
eight chickpea cultivars using two complementary protein extraction
solvents. The total protein, starch, and soluble sugar contents significantly
differ between cultivars, and we quantified 2434 and 1809 proteins,
respectively, from urea- and water-based extraction solvents using
a data-independent acquisition approach. The proteome-level differences
can vary from 9–25% for the urea-extracted proteins, and the
storage protein abundances significantly differed between the cultivars,
where legumin content was detected as the highest, followed by vicilin
and albumin. Fifty common allergens were detected from two extraction
solvents, primarily overrepresented in chromosomes 3, 4, and 5. Integrated
analysis revealed distinct subclusters of proteins and their associated
pathways for total protein, lipids, and starch content. Overall, we
established chickpea pan-proteome resources and provided insights
into the key pathways that define the genotypes.

Materials and Methods
2.1
Chickpea Samples
Eight Desi chickpea
varieties: Ambar, Genesis 509, Genesis 836, PBA HatTrick, Neelam,
PBA Captain, PBA Drummond and PBA Striker were used for the proteome
analysis in the present study. The chickpea cultivar details and seed
phenotypes have been documented previously.
23
Seeds were sourced from plants grown under common glasshouse conditions
in Perth, Western Australia (31°56′58.5″S 115°47′23.6″E).
2.2
Seed Processing and Flour Preparation
Twenty-five seeds per line were soaked in 20 mL of water at 4 °C
overnight. Seed coats were then removed by hand and seeds were dried
at 40 °C for 48 h. Dried, decorticated seeds were milled in a
TissueLyzer II (Qiagen) with a 3 cm ball bearing at 25 Hz for 30 s.
Flours were stored in airtight containers at room temperature until
use. These ground seed flour samples were used for the subsequent
analysis.
2.3
Soluble Sugar, Starch, and Protein Measurement
Soluble sugars were extracted from 10 mg of flour by ethanol. The
soluble sugar supernatant was assayed using anthrone.
24
The remaining insoluble fraction was then analyzed for
starch content using an enzymatic assay (Megazyme). Following starch
solubilization and analysis, the insoluble pellet was incubated with
proteinase K (Sigma-Aldrich, Australia) overnight at 37 °C before
being spun at 16,000
g
. The pellet was washed by resuspending
in 80% (v/v) ethanol twice, then frozen at −80 °C. The
frozen pellet was then freeze-dried and weighed. This was the insoluble
fiber fraction.
2.4
Protein Extraction from Chickpea Flour
2.4.1
Urea-Thiourea-CHAPS (UTC)-Based Protein
Extraction Buffer
Proteins were extracted from the eight
chickpea flour samples using a modified urea-based buffer (8 M urea,
2 M thiourea, 4% CHAPS and 50 mM DTT).
21
The samples (20 mg) were added to 200 μL of extraction buffer
with 5 replicates for each. The samples were vortexed, sonicated for
5 min in a sonic water bath, and shaken at 1000 rpm for 30 min at
room temperature (RT) in a thermomixer. The supernatant was harvested
following centrifugation (20,800
g
, 15 min). The protein
concentration was determined using a colorometric Bradford protein
assay.
2.4.2
Alkaline Water-Based Protein Extraction
Buffer
Water-soluble proteins were extracted from the eight
chickpea flour samples using a water dispersal fractionation.
25
The 20 mg of pea powder sample was dissolved
in 200 μL of alkaline water at a ratio of 1:10 (Ultrapure, Thermo
Fischer Scientific pH 9.0 adjusted with 1 M NaOH) in 2.0 mL tube.
The tubes were vortexed until the flour was adequately mixed with
the solution and shaken in a thermomixer (1400 rpm) at RT for 1 h
to obtain uniform dispersions. The water flour dispersions were submitted
to a low-speed centrifugation step at 4000
g
for 10
min. During this step, the insoluble starch granules were separated
into the pellet. The supernatant is referred to as the protein-rich
fraction (PRF), and the pellet is the starch-rich fraction (SRF).
26
The starch-containing pellet was again washed
and treated for 45 min with water pH 9.0 (flour to water ratio 1:5)
by adding 100 μL of alkaline water on a thermomixer at 1400
rpm and centrifuged at 4000
g
for 10 min. The protein-rich
fractions obtained from the first 1:10 and the second 1:5 alkaline
water extraction for individual samples were pooled for the downstream
analysis, and the starch pellet was discarded. The supernatant dispersions
(milky supernatant) containing the protein-rich fraction were assessed
for protein concentration using a Bradford protein assay.
2.5
Tryptic Digestion
Protein was subjected
to filter-assisted sample preparation (FASP) wherein the protein extract
(100 μg) was applied to a 10 kDa molecular weight cutoff (MWCO)
filter (Millipore, Australia) and centrifuged at 20,800
g
for 15 min. Protein digestion steps were described in detail previously.
21
2.6
Global Proteome Measurement Using Data Dependent
Acquisition Workflow
The resultant digested peptides were
resuspended in 0.1% formic acid and analyzed by LC-MS/MS as previously
described.
27
In brief, proteolytically
digested proteins were analyzed with chromatographic separation (4
μL, equivalent to 4 μg) on an Ekspert nanoLC415 (Eksigent,
Dublin, CA) directly coupled to the OptiFlow ion source of a TripleTOF
6600 LC-MS/MS (SCIEX, Redwood City, CA).
2.7
Chickpea Database Preparation and Database
Searching
Raw spectral data files were processed using ProteinPilot
5.0 software (SCIEX) with integrated false discovery rate analysis
and the Paragon Algorithm (2) was used for protein identification.
Tandem mass spectrometry data was searched against a custom-built
database comprising four chickpea genomes (GenBank accessions: GCA_000331145.1,
GCA_006151565.1, GCA_006345785.1, GCA_000347275.4) appended to the
UniProt chickpea database (version 20230331) and a database of contaminant
proteins known as the common repository of adventitious proteins (cRAP).
28
The custom database contained 213,164 proteins
after removing redundant sequences. The identification of proteins
was recorded at the confidence level, i.e., of a 1% global false discovery
rate (FDR).
2.9
SWATH-MS Data Acquisition
The individual
digested protein extracts (4.0 μL of sample equivalent to 4
μg of peptide) were chromatographically separated as described
previously. To monitor and evaluate the stability of the system, a
pooled sample was inserted in the sample cohort (7
n
injections), and the data consistency of this pooled biological
quality control (PBQC) was evaluated. The mass spectrometry instrument
performance was monitored by injecting β gal digest (AB SIEX)
in every ten experimental samples. During data acquisition, samples
were randomized, and blank samples (0.1% formic acid) were injected
between individual samples to remove any carry-over effect. The MS
source conditions were also identical. The TOF-MS survey scan was
collected over the mass range of
m
/
z
400–1250 with a 50 ms accumulation time, and the product
ion mass spectra were acquired over the mass range of
m
/
z
100–1400 with a 30 ms accumulation time.
Variable window SWATH ranges were determined using the SWATH variable
window calculator 1.0 (SCIEX) to identify 100 optimal ranges (including
1 Da overlap) spanning
m
/
z
100–1400,
resulting in a 3.1 s cycle time. Collision energy (CE) was determined
using each window center as the input
m
/
z
for CE equations and a CE spread of 5 eV was used to allow for
m
/
z
variance across each SWATH window.
Spectra were acquired using Analyst TF v1.8.1 software. Preliminary
spectral analysis visualizing the total ion chromatograms was performed
using PeakView (SCIEX).
2.10
Protein Quantitation Using DIA-NN Software
Raw SWATH-MS data files were processed using the DIA-Neural Network
(DIA-NN) software suite
29
in a library-free
mode, as described previously.
30
This search
resulted in the peptide and protein abundance data matrix across the
eight chickpea varieties.
2.11
Data Pretreatment, Missing Value Imputation,
Statistical and Bioinformatics Analysis
The resultant peptide
data matrix detected at 1% FDR was used to compare the extraction
protocols. The resulting protein data matrices were uploaded to MetaboAnalyst
6.0 and iDEP 2.01 software for missing value imputation. We used the
KNN (feature-wise) algorithm and selected the “removed features
with >50% missing values” for the missing value imputation.
Then, we used log 10 data transformation and Pareto scaling
prior to multivariate data analysis. The Principal Component Analysis
(PCA) was initially performed to evaluate the proteome data quality.
The correlation analysis (higher
r
value represents
less variability between samples during data acquisition) between
PBQCs were used as an indicator for proteome data quality checking.
The processed data matrices were downloaded for statistical and bioinformatics
analysis. The univariate analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism
v10.1 and the clustering analyses used Morpheus software (
https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus/
). The Principal Component Analysis was performed using iDEP 2.01
software (
http://bioinformatics.sdstate.edu/idep/
). The module–trait relationships were investigated using
the (WGCNA)
31
on the MiBiOmics software
platform.
32
The trait–module relationships
and variable in importance (VIP) scores were curated and visualized
in Morpheus software (
https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus/
). The functional analyses were performed using OmicsBox software
v3.0.30 and STRING-db online (
https://string-db.org/
).
2.12
Allergen Predictions
Identified
sequences were subjected to
in silico
allergen predictions.
First, linear IgE epitopes with confirmed immune reactivity were retrieved
from the Immune Epitope Database (
www.iedb.org
). Additionally, all quantified proteins were also
investigated for allergens using AllerCatPro software.
33
Proteins with 100% allergen epitope sequence
similarity and strong evidence were included in the analysis. Based
on the predicted epitopes, the sequences were mapped to the quantified
protein sequences using a 100% sequence match in CLC Genomics Workbench
v. Twenty-four (QIAGEN, Aarhus, Denmark).
2.13
Chromosomal Mapping and Circos Plot Visualization
Circos plot was used to show the average abundance values and chromosomal
position of quantified proteins from two extraction solvents (Urea–Tris–HCL
(UTC) and water (WT) extraction solvents) on the chickpea reference
genome chromosomes. ShinyCircos, a R/Shiny application, was used to
construct a chromosome-based Circos plot.
34
UniProtKB accession IDs of quantified proteins were converted to
RefSeq protein IDs and gene IDs using the chickpea reference genome
and translated gene models retrieved from the National Centre for
Biotechnology Information (NCBI) (Genome assembly ASM33114v1).
14
The chromosomal location and exact position
of the mapped proteins and allergens were collected from the chickpea
reference genome and used to annotate the Circos plot. To construct
two heatmap panels, log 10-adjusted protein abundance of SWATH-MS
results of two applied extraction protocols for eight varieties were
used.

3.1
Experimental Samples and Study Design
In this study, we measured the composition of seed macromolecules
and proteomes of eight desi chickpea cultivars. Complementary water-
and UTC-based extraction solvents were used for protein extraction.
The data-independent acquisition method was used to quantify the proteome-level
variations between the chickpea cultivars. Finally, integrated bioinformatics
analysis was performed to discover the module–trait relationships.
A summary of the experimental design is shown in
Figure
1
A.
Figure 1
Proteomics workflow for
chickpea proteome profiling. (A) Schematic
representation of the experimental workflow for seed phenotype measurements,
proteome profiling and statistical analysis. (B) Total protein, starch
and soluble sugar content measurements across chickpea cultivars.
Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s
HSD test (
P
< 0.05).

1
Introduction
Chickpea (
Cicer arietinum
L.), a
self-pollinated annual diploid legume crop species (2
n
= 2
x
= 16), is a member of the Fabaceae family.
Legumes and pulses have been part of the human diet for centuries,
valued for their nutritional value and relatively high protein content.
1
Chickpeas have the capacity for symbiotic nitrogen
fixation to improve soil nitrogen content and rotating with other
crops can improve soil quality.
2
Chickpeas
provide a vital source of nutrients—containing 20–30%
protein and >40–60% carbohydrates and are a rich source
of
minerals and fiber.
3
Chickpeas can be broadly
categorized as Kabuli and Desi types based on their growth requirements,
markets and end-use. Kabuli chickpeas have a beige seed coat and large,
smooth seeds without edges, while Desi chickpeas have a dark-colored
coat and are small, with rough seeds.
4
,
5
The proximate
seed composition differs broadly within the species,
6
and chemical compositional variations, such as differences
in bioactive compounds, are also observed for chickpea cultivars.
7
The major types of storage proteins in legumes
are albumins (water-soluble), globulins (dilute saline soluble) and
prolamins (alcohol soluble).
8
Globulins
are classified based on their sedimentation coefficient into 7S globulins
(vicilin, convicilin) and 11S globulins (legumin, glycinin, and legumin-like).
9
These key seed storage proteins act as a reserve
of carbon and nitrogen and supply energy during germination and food
nutrition upon consumption but can also trigger immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated
allergenic reactions.
10
For example, pathogenesis-related
protein family 10, late embryogenesis abundant protein and vicilin-containing
fractions from raw and boiled chickpeas can cosensitize patients with
allergies to birch pollen and peanuts.
10
In addition, chickpea albumins (2S)
11
and globulins
12
have been shown to trigger
allergic reactions, but considerable variability exists within and
between chickpea genotypes, offering opportunities to breed low-allergen
cultivars.
13
These species-level variations
represent a rich source of phenotypic plasticity with underlying genes,
proteins and pathways that control the stress tolerance for agronomic
traits such as yield and consumer-preferred traits such as flavor.
Thus, investigating the natural diversity of these chickpea varieties
is essential to facilitate trait improvement. The molecular mechanisms
that enable chickpea interspecies variability to compositional changes
are poorly understood.
Several large-scale genomics and pan-genomics
studies have revealed
the genetic blueprint of chickpea cultivars.
14
,
15
These studies have provided insights into the global distributions
of genetic variation,
14
how this variability
affects the seed composition, and plant physiological responses to
biotic and abiotic stress.
16
In addition,
researchers have studied plant physiology, seed development and chromosomal
regions controlling agronomic traits such as disease resistance,
17
but the proteome level diversity linked to yield,
protein content and quality traits has been limited.
A limited
number of proteome-level studies have been performed
on a selected range of chickpea varieties. For instance, two-dimensional
(2D) gel and liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)
techniques were used to study the three developmental stage-specific
seed proteome and phosphoproteome changes in chickpea cultivars.
18
Likewise, gel-based techniques were applied
to investigate changes in the nuclear proteome of chickpea cultivars
under water-deficit conditions, showing the differential abundance
of proteins involved in gene transcription and replication, molecular
chaperones, cell signaling, and chromatin remodeling processes.
19
Gel electrophoresis analysis of 24 chickpea
varieties showed significant variability between storage protein content
and composition between the genotypes.
13
However, comprehensive proteome-level studies are lacking for chickpea
varieties, unlike those available for other legumes
20
and cereal crops.
21
This limits
our molecular-level understanding of how protein interactions influence
key traits, including traits valuable for breeding and enhancing health
attributes and techno-functional qualities.
Sequencing and assembly
of multiple cultivars for pan-genome studies
can accelerate proteogenomic experiments, bridging the gap between
genes and proteins. This enables further understanding of molecular
mechanisms and trait improvement. Here, we first investigated eight
chickpea cultivars by measuring their proximate composition of protein,
starch, and soluble sugar contents. Then, we used urea–thiourea–CHAPS
(UTC) and water-based protein extraction solvents to comprehensively
profile the chickpea proteome, aiming to extract the maximum number
of seed storage proteins (SSPs), as their solubility depends on the
protein extraction solvents.
22
Next, we
annotated the chickpea proteome separately for UTC and water-extracted
proteins and detected the extraction buffer-dependent protein functions
and pathways. Additionally,
in silico
allergen mapping
and chromosomal positions were established across the eight cultivars.
Finally, the weighted gene coexpression
network analysis (WGCNA) revealed the key relationship between proteins
and their measured traits, empowering the identification of pathways
potentially associated with superior agronomic traits.

Results and Discussion
3.1
Experimental Samples and Study Design

1
A.

chickpea proteome profiling. (A) Schematic
representation of the experimental workflow for seed phenotype measurements,
proteome profiling and statistical analysis. (B) Total protein, starch

3.2
Cultivar-Specific Macromolecule Composition
Differences
To understand the seed macromolecule compositions,
we measured total protein, starch and soluble sugars across eight
chickpea cultivars. As expected, the cultivars were significantly
different for total protein (
P
< 0.0001); starch
(
P
< .03) and soluble sugar (
P
< 0.0001) (one-way ANOVA analysis with Tukey’s HSD test).The
cultivar Genesis 509 contains the lowest amount of protein but the
highest starch content (
Figure
1
B), supporting the trade-off trend previously reported for
protein and starch accumulation in the seed.

Comparatively, Neelam, with the highest protein content of all tested
lines, has a ∼32% higher protein content than Genesis 509.
The total starch content variation was relatively small between cultivars,
with ∼14% difference in concentration between the highest cultivar,
Genesis 509 and the lowest, PBA Drummond. Notably, Neelam had a ∼166%
higher concentration of measured soluble sugars than observed for
PBA Drummond. These results show considerable potential for detecting
the accumulation of favorable macromolecule compositions for chickpea
cultivars.
The major legume seed reserve components, such as
protein, starch and lipid content, differ between cultivars due to
genetic variability, environmental impacts and agronomic practices.
36

and N mobilization, translocation from photosynthetic source tissues
and the strength of the pull of the sink play a key role in accumulating
these storage materials in legume seeds.

,
38

in total starch and protein content, similar to previous studies.
39
,
40
Previous studies reported total starch content ranges from 41.5
to 43.1% in PBA HatTrick and Drummond, which is ∼13% higher
than the current study.
39
This difference
is likely a product of growing conditions, with past studies reporting
different starch concentrations in other regions such as India (starch
29–35.2%).
41
Similar trends were
observed for total protein content differences between the present
study and previous experiments with PBA Drummond and Captain, where
the samples were grown in different regions across Australia.
39
While genetic factors primarily determine the
chemical composition of seeds, environmental conditions also have
the power to play a significant role in governing grain composition,
which warrants future studies combining field trials with multiomics
investigation to understand the genotype x environment influence of
seed composition.

3.5
Identification and Mapping of Allergenic Proteins
to the Chickpea Genome
Chickpea proteins can trigger allergenic
responses in humans and can cross-react with major allergens from
walnuts, peas, lentils, lupins and soy.
10
,
53
Here, we investigated
the allergenic proteins detected and quantified from both the UTC-
and water-based extracted proteomes of the 8 chickpea cultivars by
searching against sequences downloaded from the Immune Epitope Database
(IEDB) and the AllerCatPro
33
software.
Sixty allergenic proteins were identified in the water-extracted proteome;
among these, 35 were reported using linear epitopes retrieved from
IEDB, 16 using AllerCatPro, and 9 were predicted from both databases.
These proteins were mapped to 19 reference families, including soybean,
lentil, peanut, chickpea, hazelnut, almond, walnut, and chestnut (
File S1
), with 37 showing high sequence similarity
to reference allergens. These represented homologues of major allergens
from the cupin family allergens such as vicilins and legumins (Gly
m 5, Len c 1, Pis s 1, Pis s 2 and Gly m 6, Cic a 6 (10 proteins)),
60S ribosomal proteins (Pru d 5, RING-type domain-containing proteins
(7 proteins)), LEA proteins (Cic a 1 (3 proteins)) and oleosins (Ara
h 10, Ara h 11, Ara h 15 (4 proteins)). 72 allergenic proteins were
found in UTC extraction solvents, with 46 identified using linear
epitopes from IEDB, 20 identified using AllerCatPro, and 6 detected
from both databases. Notably, the detected 40 allergens mapped to
15 reference allergen families from the same species as the water
extracted proteome, with homology to the same major allergens as water
extraction, with the addition of allergens such as heat shock proteins
(Cas s 9, Cor a 10 (4 proteins)), and Bet v 1 family proteins (Gly
m 4, (6 proteins)) (
File S2
). These allergenic
proteins were subsequently mapped to the chickpea genome, providing
a chromosomal perspective on their distribution. The detected allergens,
which mapped to known reference allergens from UTC and water-extracted
solvents, were primarily overrepresented in chromosomes 3, 4, and
5 (
Figure
4
). Understanding
the abundance and chromosomal location of potential allergenic proteins
may contribute knowledge to the potential health risks of the grains and
the breeding of low allergenic lines in the future.

The cultivar-specific
proteome level analysis generated in this
study provides a valuable resource for chickpea quality trait identification,
highlighted herein allergen mapping
and association analysis with seed
macromolecule measurements. We underscore the
power of proteome-level discovery and integration studies to identify
pathways associated with important agronomic traits such as protein
content and provide insight into broader species-level diversification
trends. Our study focused on a comparative analysis of proteins and
pathways; however, additional protein characterization methods, such
as post-translational modifications and processing of proteins in
different ways, are also important factors in the diversification
of chickpea crops and should be the focus of future research.
We have shown that cultivars with increased chaperone activities,
such as HSPs, are associated with higher protein content (
Figure
6
). Future breeding
or engineering activities in chickpeas will have
to consider not only target genes for high protein content but also
processes such as protein folding and amino acid metabolism to support
the accumulation of these proteins. Additionally, identifying several
chickpea HSPs as potential allergens in this analysis highlights the
value of proteomics work in assisting target selection for crop improvement.
Our analyses underscore the power of proteome-level discovery and
integration studies to identify pathways associated with important
agronomic traits such as protein content, and provide insight into
broader species-level diversification trends.
In addition to
genetic controls of traits like protein content,
future studiesexploring different management practices,
such as applying low or high-nitrogen fertilizer for seed yield and
quality variations, would be beneficial. Furthermore, the detected
protein sequences can be assessed for their allergenicity by using
advanced prediction models,
61
expressing
recombinant proteins of these putative chickpea allergens and testing
